beats.content:
In a block theme, every part of the site is built from blocks: the header, the list of posts, the footer, all of it.

Its templates are plain `.html` files full of **block markup**, which WordPress reads and turns into the page. For example, this one line outputs the site's title on any WordPress site:

```html
<!-- wp:site-title /-->
```

Because everything is blocks, people using your theme can change any of it visually in the Site Editor (**Appearance > Editor**). WordPress also writes the `<html>`, `<head>` and `<body>` tags for you, so your templates only describe what goes inside the page.
beats.goal: See what makes a block theme different.
beats.question: Which part of a site would you most like to be able to change with blocks?

beats.content:
WordPress needs just two files to recognise a block theme:

- `style.css` in the theme's root folder. Its header comment holds the theme's details, such as its name and description.
- `templates/index.html`. This is the default, fallback template. Having it is what makes WordPress treat the theme as a block theme.

Everything else is optional, though most themes use more of it:

```text
my-block-theme/
  parts/        reusable sections, like header.html
  patterns/     block patterns, registered automatically
  styles/       style variations (extra JSON files)
  templates/
    index.html  (required)
  style.css     (required)
  theme.json    settings and styles
```

Some older tutorials say a block theme also needs `index.php`. Current WordPress doesn't: `style.css` plus `templates/index.html` is enough.
beats.goal: Know the two files every block theme needs.
beats.question: If you deleted templates/index.html, what do you think WordPress would make of the theme?

beats.goal: Meet theme.json, the theme's control centre.
beats.question: Why might a typo in theme.json be harder to notice than a typo in CSS?

bug.explanation: The Contrast entry used "value" where theme.json expects "color". Palette entries take exactly "name", "slug" and "color", and WordPress reads each colour from "color". Without it, WordPress skips the entry, so no "--wp--preset--color--contrast" property is created, and nothing warns you. AI assistants make this kind of slip often, which is why it's worth checking their theme.json against the schema. Your fixed file is now your theme's theme.json.

fixChecks.message: Every palette entry should use the same three keys. Look for the entry that doesn't match the others.
Keep the Contrast colour's hex code exactly as it was. Only the key around it is wrong.
The file must keep version 3, and the Contrast entry must end up with the same keys as the others. Check for a missing comma or quote.

checkpoint.question: In a sentence or two, which two files does every block theme need, and what does each one do?
checkpoint.rubric: Advance if the answer names both style.css (it holds the theme's details, such as its name, in a header comment) and templates/index.html (the default or fallback template, which makes WordPress treat the theme as a block theme). The roles can be described loosely. Review if it names only one of the two, names theme.json, functions.php or index.php as required, or is unsure. Skip only if the answer gets both right and also correctly explains extra detail, such as theme.json settings versus styles, or that theme.json is optional.
